newsitem.title: UK: Away from oil, Iraq raid leaves commodities cold.
newsitem.headline: Away from oil, Iraq raid leaves commodities cold.

text.p: The U.S. raid on Iraq left commodity markets outside the petroleum sector unmoved on Tuesday.

Gold either no longer enjoyed its traditional role as a "safe haven" in time of tension, or investors weren't worried enough about events in the Middle East to feel they needed one. Either way, the bullion price edged up about 50 cents an ounce on early buying in Asia then eased to fix in the London afternoon at $386.60 -- hardly changed from Monday. Other commodity prices were also flat with markets unconcerned by the Iraq problem unless this should escalate, although the likely delay to the U.N. oil-for-food deal with Iraq may soon add to downward pressure on grain prices.
Commodity traders assumed that the new hostilities would mean indefinite delay on implementing the agreement to ease the United Nations Gulf War oil embargo on Iraq.

The deal would have allowed sales worth $2 billion over six months to buy food and medicine -- with grain and sugar high on Iraq's shopping list. "This is not good for the market," said a Paris grain trader. "But I expect only limited pressure on already-easier world prices."
Prices have slipped in recent weeks on news of good harvests in several regions.

Benchmark Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) wheat futures were scarely changed on the day at around $4.50 a bushel, down from a record $7.50 in March during a "spike" that followed drought in Australia, Russia and North Africa. Another trader said there had been more talk than actual deals on selling grain to Iraq amid arguments over how the U.N. accord would perform. Sugar imports by private Iraqi traders are likely to be reduced during the present crisis but sugar is expected to continue to enter Iraq via Jordan, sugar industry sources said.
They added that delay on the U.N. oil-for-food plan would not dramatically affect the volume of sugar already entering the country so long as it can use Jordan's Red Sea port of Aqaba.
"Sugar has been going in through back doors anyway but (the U.S. raid) is not going to make it any cheaper," said Chris Pack, senior analyst at Czarnikow Sugar.
